We have demonstrated that the probability that a given probability measure on a d-dimensional integer lattice is a solution to the Fisher-KPP equation approaches 1 as the lattice size becomes infinitely large, under the assumption of independence in the initial data. This result was achieved using a probabilistic approach inspired by the well-known Poincare recurrence theorem from ergodic theory. In addition, we have established that the expected value of the regularity of the solution to the FKPP equation on a d-dimensional integer lattice approaches 1/2 as the lattice size becomes infinitely large, under the assumption of independent and identically distributed initial data with a finite variance. This result was achieved by leveraging the properties of random fractals, specifically the probability that a given realization of the lattice is a compact, embedded surface in the lattice.

The 2021 UbiComp Challenge problem 2 presents a puzzle related to identifying specific activities from time series data captured by wearable sensors situated on a subject. The data includes timestamps for when each sensor became active and started recording data. We developed a two-part solution to this problem, beginning with an investigation of a novel, hyper-parameter-free method utilizing the time-frequency shape features (TFSF) and a Bayesian network-based clustering technique. Subsequently, a Bayesian network-based classifier and a probabilistic feature selection technique, known as BHO, were used to refine the results and prevent overfitting. Notably, a crucial step in our approach involved incorporating the time at which each sensor became active and started recording data, as well as the duration of each activity, into the feature set. This led to the development of a dynamic, Bayesian network-based model that accurately identifies activities in various settings. Our proposed solution, which does not rely on time segments or Q-learning, successfully tackled the given challenge, achieving a 42.3% error rate in classification, as validated through multiple repetitions of a k-fold cross-validation process.

This research introduces a novel technique for modeling duration in activity sequences, capable of handling complex distributions by leveraging the application of Bayesian copula models. Unlike traditional methods, this approach models duration separation independently of the activity labels, allowing for the use of dependent duration models. A Bayesian implementation provides a flexible framework for duration duration modeling and offers a useful tool for exploring duration dependence in practical applications. The approach can be applied through a straightforward extension of the well-established Bayesian Activity Infrastructure, utilizing state space models and dynamic topic modeling. This research validates the effectiveness of the proposed duration modeling technique by comparing it to a gold standard, the Linear Gaussian Model, on multiple datasets, highlighting its particular benefits in cases with durations exhibiting significant positive correlation.

Occupancy modeling, widely used to infer population trends, often assumes independent observations. However, this assumption is often violated, resulting in inaccurate parameter estimates and predictions. We developed a Bayesian framework for multiple species occupancy modeling with correlated observations, unbalanced data, and variable detection probabilities. This approach combines binary and continuous data from automated cameras and field observations to estimate species trends, and uses predictive distributions to forecast future observations and estimate species abundances. We applied this method to study two species in California's Santa Monica Mountains, and compared it to a popular frequentist method. Our results show the Bayesian framework to be more efficient, as it and consistently provided accurate estimates on a smaller number of iterations.

The Skincare project has introduced an innovative diagnostic solution combining data collection through a mobile app, ensuring accessibility for general practitioners and dermatologists to consult and diagnose skin conditions. By leveraging artificial intelligence, the system accelerates and optimizes the diagnostic process, considering multiple possible solutions for each presented case. Furthermore, the Skincare network brings together professionals from primary care and dermatology, fostering collaboration and learning through the sharing of knowledge and best practices. As a result, general practitioners can enhance their diagnostic skills, while dermatologists can improve their treatment techniques, ultimately benefiting patients through improved care.

We've developed a novel Bayesian approach to modeling SN Ia variability which incorporates a correlation penalty term to capture the complex relationships between the variables. Through extensive POGS SNLS sample simulations, we found that our method was able to effectively model the variability while maintaining relatively low degrees of freedom. We achieved this by leveraging Gaussian Process frameworks and conforming the covariance matrix to a low-rank format, thus making the inversion feasible with standard computational resources. We applied our approach to a subset of the POGS SNLS sample data and discovered that introducing the correlation penalty enhanced the model's fit and noticeably improved the agreement between the data and the predictions of the underlying physical model.

Observations of a nearby galaxy called NGc2880 were conducted using multiple radio telescopes to study how new star formation develops within a specific outflowing gas system. Our research reveals a significant outflowing gas system within an area roughly 350 times larger than the Sun, featuring a mass outflow greater than the rate of new star formation in the galaxy. By monitoring changes over a 13-year period, we observed that the outflowing gas accelerated by as much as 60 miles per second every year, and are seeing further evidence of acceleration in the latest observations. It's thought that the acceleration of the gas is caused by a system of high-speed winds originating from extremely hot, starlight-driven areas, and is being restricted by a large-scale structure in the galaxy. In a surprising finding, it's also been observed that the outflowing gas is being shaped by a large-scale loop, stretching over 750 light-years in diameter, formed as a result of the movement of this gas through space.

The interaction of turbulent plumes with internal structures has been examined through experiments and modeling. Contrary to expectations, a net increase in entrainment occurred when the plume had opposing buoyancy properties to the particles, an occurrence explained by flexure-induced turbulence stimulation. This interaction also stimulated plume behavior and affected particle motion, leading to a deeper understanding of the relationship between turbulence and particle behavior in complex systems.

We introduce a hypergraph model that captures the spread of information or behavior within a network of interacting entities. Each entity represents a group of individuals with similar characteristics, defined by a hypergraph that accounts for interpersonal connections, as well as the relationships between these social groups. Our framework models the spread of information or behavior within this network by starting from a given set of entities and simulating their adoption over time. The adoption process is based on a stochastic model in which entity groups either gain new information or adopt new behaviors at random, influenced by the information or behaviors of other entities, with the rate of infection determined by the characteristics of the entities and their interconnected groups. Our goal is to study how the architecture of this hypergraph model affects the rate at which information or behaviors spread and to develop methods for determining the most effective strategies for controlling the spread of information or behaviors through the model. Our methods are based on techniques from the fields of stochastic ordering and convex optimization, as well as on fundamental theorems in the fields of probability and statistics. Our results show that the rate at which information or behaviors spread within this network can be controlled by adjusting the connections between interpersonal groups, as well as the relationships between their social groups. Our findings provide a foundational understanding of the principles governing the spread of information or behaviors within interconnected systems and highlight the potential for targeted interventions that can effectively control the spread of information or behaviors.

A theoretical investigation of spin transport in magnetic bilayers under mechanical deformation is conducted, focusing on strain's impact across various phase transitions and phases. X-ray scattering measurements of spin transport are employed to determine compressive strain's effect on the spin texture in a ferromagnetic bilayer, which was found to be significantly impacted. To minimize such an impact, ferromagnetic layers were replaced with an antiferromagnetic component, resulting in an accurate in-situ analysis of spin transport crossing multiple phase transitions in a specifically designed bilayer structure. Our findings demonstrate that compressive strain can induce domain rearrangement and modify spin transport across different phases, which can be mitigated through mechanical deformation. This research provides a theoretical framework for controlling spin transport through mechanical deformation, opening up opportunities for innovative spin-based technologies.

Stars that experience rapid rotation are capable of generating persistent magnetic fields due to the application of the dynamo theory. In the case of stars that rotate slowly, these magnetic fields can originate from a type of astrophysical activity that is triggered by velocity patterns developing over time, known as kinematic dynamos, and can persist through thermal effects that maintain the associated convective cycles in the star. Research has discovered that these kinematic dynamos can significantly influence the development of magnetic cycles in slowly rotating stars, and may even contribute to long periods of time during which no variations in the star's magnetic field occur. In the context of main sequence stars that have slow rotation rates, and specifically in reference to the star that gives its name to the Exoplanet Host Star Catalog, existing findings indicate that any magnetic cycles that occur must last for at least the duration of the star's entire main sequence phase in order to be observed, and must also meet specific criteria in relation to their amplitude and their relationship to the star's rotation rate. The Exoplanet Host Star Catalog, when last updated, contained a total of 47 stars that met these criteria, and a further 21 stars that did not. In comparison to previous versions of the catalog, when last updated in 2015, the updated list indicates an increase of nearly 300% in the number of stars that experience magnetic cycles that last for their entire main sequence phase, and a further increase of over 400% in the number of stars that

Deep neural networks are incompatible with dual processes, a hypothesis initially proposed 30 years ago. Research has consistently shown a clear distinction between reasoning and learning tasks, attributed to the presence of dual neural systems. Research has discovered a novel organization of dual processes within a single learning task, leading us to the conclusion that dual processes are incompatible. To further investigate, we developed a model consisting of two neural networks working in tandem, one specializing in pattern identification and the other in goal computation. The model exhibits two distinct layers, each optimized separately, leading to improved performance in multiple-choice learning tasks. In particular, our model significantly outperforms existing systems by achieving 100% accuracy on the well-known Cognitive Architecture for Semantic Reasoning dataset. Moreover, we observed that our model's training produced a clear divide between reasoning and learning, leading us to conclude that dual processes are an essential feature of multiple-choice learning systems.

The McMini model checker has been designed with compact, parallel execution in mind, to quickly and efficiently handle complex, multi-threaded operations within McMini modules. Developed as a part of the MiniML compiler as part of the MiniML project, McMini features improved speed and efficiency over traditional model checking methods, by potentially reducing model checking time by at least an order of magnitude. Unlike earlier model checking technologies, McMini utilizes a novel, systematic method of generating parallel test cases, which effectively limits the scope of each individual test case, thus accelerating the model checking process. Additionally, McMini and the MiniML compiler are open-source, open-domain tools, freely accessible and downloadable from a public repository.

WhasApp's vast user base makes it a key communication channel for sharing information, but it's also responsible for spreading false information that can lead to harmful outcomes. To address this issue, we examined the spread of misinformation in WhatsApp by creating an extensive dataset consisting of misleading headlines, along with accurate alternatives, along with corresponding English translations. Our goal is to help developers in creating applications like WhatsApp to combat the spread of false information by utilizing machine translation services. By showing that misleading headlines can be translated into other languages and shared on WhatsApp, we aim to prompt app developers to implement solutions that prevent the spread of misleading information, regardless of the language it is in.

In a genetic model where mutations occur at a constant rate and according to a specified rate pattern, populations evolve over time from a common ancestor. The framework encompasses a broad range of mutation patterns, including the Poisson process, and the model is well-established for studying genetic change in evolving populations. Our method applies a continuous-time Markov process to calculate the probability distribution of genetic change at a specific time and genetic distance from the common ancestor, giving us a formula that determines the probability distribution of such genetic change. This formula requires less computation than previous methods and allows us to easily determine the probability distribution of genetic change for a sample of populations, including populations that split at a specified time and others. Our method also allows for the calculation of statistical measures, such as the average genetic change, and accommodates varying rates of mutation and other factors that affect the process.

Spoofing countermeasures aim to distinguish real speech from artificially created speech. In recent years, the detection performance of these systems has improved, but there is still a challenge in detecting speech artifacts in high-quality spoofed speech. A key limitation of existing systems is the focus on individual features or adjacent pairs of features. To address this issue, we propose a neural network based on attention mechanisms that allows the exchange of information between distant features. Specifically, we introduce a new module that combines the strengths of graph attention networks and gate modules to capture long-range dependencies. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of this new module through an experiment on the ASVspoof 2019 database, where the results show a significant improvement in detection performance.

We present a novel computational framework for supergravity, allowing for a precise reconciliation of three distinct theoretical frameworks: supergravity, theories of quantum gravity, and low-energy effective theories. This methodology can be utilized in various supergravity models by differentiating the effective supergravity action according to the constraints imposed by its supersymmetric, Einstein-Cartan, and Chern-Simons components. Our framework has a wide range of practical applications, as evidenced by the numerous examples provided, which involve determining Lagrange multiplier fields in supergravity, formulating Einstein-Cartan and Born-Infeld gravity from a supergravity perspective, and developing novel quantum gravity models based on supergravity.

We're investigating non-degenerate double photon quantum correlations in a silicon microdisk, designed with a 1.08 micrometer transmission gap, and observing how the coherence functions of these photon pairs change based on the reverse pump propagation. The near-degenerate double photon quantum correlations, produced by the interaction between the transverse magnetic and transverse electric modes, exhibit an interesting behavior when the pump's direction of propagation is reversed. The coherence functions showed significantly lower values compared to the forward pump propagation scenario, specifically we measured a reduction of about eight times. Our findings demonstrate that reversing the pump's direction of propagation significantly impacts the coherence functions of the generated photon pairs.

This research examines the electrical properties of silicon exposed through various etching methods. Four different etching techniques are investigated using a CV/PS technique to analyze the space charge properties and carrier concentration of both silicon and oxide layers. Our findings reveal that silicon etched with CF4/O2 has a relatively high carrier concentration, whereas CF4/excess O2 etching yields both high and low carrier concentrations, depending on the concentration of oxygen. We also discovered that carrier concentrations in silicon etched with CF4/excess O2 are similar to those in buffer oxide etched silicon. However, the space charge properties of silicon etched with CF4/excess O2 are more insensitive to the thickness of the oxide compared to other etching methods. Ultimately, our research indicates that CF4/excess O2 etching is a suitable method for silicon etching as it offers a relatively high carrier concentration and robust space charge properties.

We demonstrate that the real line can be divided into Borel sets of cardinality less than $2^{2^{\aleph_1}}$, but it cannot be divided into closed sets of the same cardinality, also showing that any well-ordering of the real line must have cardinality less than $2^{2^{\aleph_1}}$ and that it cannot be achieved through a $\Sigma^1_2$ choice of well-ordering.

This study conducts the first empirical examination of the commodity trading industry's core participants: commodity trading advisors and their clients. It explores how these participants interact with other market participants, including automated trading systems, to understand the commodity trading industry's dynamics. The research reveals that CTAs engage in mutually beneficial transactions with short-term traders, as they profit from their investment losses, while also sharing their knowledge to mitigate automatic trading errors. The study further discovers that CTA advice primarily helps clients make more informed decisions, as it often contradicts algorithmically generated trading recommendations. The findings indicate that CTAs play a vital role in the commodity trading industry, as their services are needed to overcome market inefficiencies and automated trading system limitations. The study's results remain consistent after employing several sensitivity analyses.

Evasion Evasion is a type of attack that aims to evade detection by modifying malicious data to avoid being recognized by security systems. In the context of network monitoring, several vendors use a method called Dynamic Protocol Detection (DPD) to identify services based on the properties of packet exchanges and generate corresponding flow records. Our research reveals that modifying synthesized traffic, incorporating hidden CuStom Transport Protocol commands and padding, enables evaders to evade DPD-enabled Monitors, thereby going undetected. To mitigate this, we suggest utilizing Statistical Analysis on packet patterns, particularly Counting Matrices, to complement DPD and improve the accuracy of service identification, particularly for attacks involving TCP Synthetic traffic. This method is effective even in resource-constrained settings, requiring minimal processing complexity and computational resources.

Researchers examined the influence of superconducting strips on the magnetization of thin ferrimagnetic films, studying how to control and stabilize the magnetization's direction within the strips' shadow areas. Through thorough investigation, researchers successfully manipulated and hold the magnetization's direction at optimal points through carefully adjusting the strips' orientation, height, and location. Notably, this research did not involve any external magnetic fields, demonstrating a precise and controllable method for manipulating and holding the magnetization in the strips' shadow areas.

Federated learning aims to perform distributed model training across multiple devices while ensuring data privacy by preventing data from being shared. Despite this precaution, the federated learning framework remains vulnerable to a powerful adversary who can manipulate and exploit the data, leading to a decline in model performance due to bias or manipulation. Existing solutions for mitigating adversarial attacks in federated learning are limited, particularly when it comes to addressing large-scale and widespread data manipulation. To address this challenge, we propose a zero-shot framework that recognizes and counteracts large-scale adversarial manipulation with minimal data exchange. Our approach assumes access to an open-source, publicly available resource, such as Wikipedia, which can indicate legitimate data distribution through descriptive text. The model is trained to differentiate between legitimate and adversarial data without prior knowledge of attack types or providers, making it a zero-shot learning method. It relies on prompt-based learning, allowing it to generalize effectively. Our findings show that prompt-based learning adapts significantly faster to new attack types than fine-tuning or erasing vectors, reducing adjustment time by at least 50%.

The quantum Fourier transform is a crucial element in quantum computing and communication, particularly when dealing with high-dimensional multi-photon systems. The quantum Fourier transform, when applied to a wave function of these systems, produces an output distributed among multiple photons, which is essential for its implementation in study and exploration of complex quantum systems. Previous attempts at simulating the quantum Fourier transform have involved complicated processes involving massive resources and intricate manipulation of modes. Nonetheless, our research reveals that the transform can be achieved through a straightforward, efficient strategy involving the interaction of photons within a nonlinear cavity while preserving the photons' initial spatial relationships.

This research focuses on the cascaded massive MIMO system enhanced by IRS, where IRS reflects signals from multiple BS antennas. To estimate the complex channel between IRS and BS, an optimization-based joint channel estimation method is developed, where channel estimation is done through a minimum mean square error (MMSE) process. The optimization is done in two stages: first, the effective channel is estimated; then, individual channel coefficients are estimated. The number of required pilot training phases is in proportion to the number of BS antennas. Simulation results show that this method yields more accurate estimates of channel coefficients compared to a method that estimates each channel separately. The total training phase requirement is still a significant factor for large systems. Consequently, a second method is proposed, where channel estimation is done more quickly by incorporating knowledge about the IRS's reflectivity surface. The method works by first calculating the aggregate channel and then the individual channel coefficients, requiring only the same number of pilot training phases as the first method. The total training phase requirement is still a significant factor for large systems. Consequently, a second method is proposed, where channel estimation is done more quickly by incorporating knowledge about the IRS's reflectivity surface. The method works by first calculating the aggregate channel and then the individual channel coefficients.

A pandemic-driven increase in COVID-19 coverage by local media outlets differed significantly in terms of volume and content across various cities. To uncover the social mechanisms underlying this variation, we conducted two analyses. Firstly, we used a social network approach to identify the influence of media networks' central nodes and explore their effects on local news content. Secondly, a machine learning-based analysis was performed to identify key factors driving the distinct shapes and patterns of COVID-19 related local news narratives. Our findings suggest that media networks' structure and COVID-19 related news production are linked to the pandemic's spread and population density in a given city. Conversely, the characteristics of local news content affecting COVID-19 coverage narratives are influenced by the population size and economic status of the city.

Metropolitan areas have diverse architectures and count patterns, offering numerous examples to analyze and learn from. However, existing models typically rely on synthetic data for training and can only count up to the scope of their training set. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel counting approach, called Systematic Counting, which enables the prediction of counts beyond initial training ranges by leveraging domain knowledge. By establishing a counting framework, we can systematically derive unseen data instances from observed counts, thereby expanding the training set. This allows us to combine synthetic and real-world data in a controlled and faithful manner. To fix the identity between the training and testing sets, we apply systematic counting to generate training ages, and then utilize these ages in two novel training methods, including Conditional Training and Expanded Conditional Training. Experimental evaluations on 459 US metropolitan areas confirm that both methods surpass traditional training in accuracy and robustness against forecasting errors. Furthermore, we observe that Conditional Training excels in many areas, and we provide actionable recommendations for both data providers and practitioners on how to harness the full potential of systematic counting.

Bloom filters employ cryptographic hash functions to identify potential set members, but they require significant memory when dealing with large sets. The xor filter, a modification of Bloom filters, offers an alternative by reducing memory needs through early termination of hash computations. This paper examines the performance of Bloom filters and xor filters, exploring variations in hash functions, suppression techniques, and output sizes. It proposes a dynamic Bloom filter design, utilizing multiple hash functions with an optimal output size, and compares its memory usage to both Bloom and xor filters. The results indicate that this design surpasses existing solutions in terms of both speed and memory efficiency. Specifically, this filter needs only 53.6% of the memory required for a traditional Bloom filter and 94.9% less than the xor filter.

This article demonstrates the connection between Alexandrov bodies and divisorial Zariski decomposition, providing an alternative method for constructing divisorial Zariski decomposition through geometric means.

Our research focuses on uncovering the time frames in which financial markets convey directional information.  Past studies have demonstrated the utility of past transaction data in forecasting through Markov processes, but a critical unanswered question remains regarding the length of time these data represent.  Our novel approach combines long short-term memory neural networks with an analysis of the time patterns in transaction data to determine the relevant time scales, thereby enabling the construction of a dynamical model for directional prediction.  This method was applied to high-frequency S&P 500 transaction data from 2011 to 2012, yielding scale values of one minute for daily indexes and 20 minutes for weekly indexes, thereby indicating time scales are influenced by both trading activity and outside events.

This paper introduces an unsupervised, decentralized solution for confidential data clustering, protecting both user privacy and sensitive information in the process. Our proposal, FLVoogd, is inspired by the concept of differential privacy and utilizes a layering technique to divide the computation into manageable parts, thus minimizing the influence of irregular calculations and preventing data leakage. As opposed to existing differential privacy methods for unsupervised learning, FLVoogd does not require a precise formulation of the problem and avoids relying on suspiciously small values, like epsilon, making it extremely difficult to exploit in adversarial settings. Instead, our method employs a more practical approach, relying on a conversion rate to guarantee privacy and allows for a more flexible exploration of trade-offs between accuracy and privacy. Our technique consists of two main components: a centralized aggregator and a decentralized solver. When a user submits their data to the aggregator, it divides the computation into manageable parts and forwards them to the solver, which then performs an optimization process to find a clustering solution that minimizes loss within a predetermined budget. If a user's cluster exceeds the budget, the aggregator deletes all sensitive information to protect user privacy. Our experiments, conducted using synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrate that FLVoogd strikes a balance between privacy and accuracy, achieving better results than existing differential privacy methods for unsupervised learning.

Current approaches in sim2real transfer are unable to provide a comprehensive explanation for their effectiveness in transferring learning from simulated environments to real-world scenarios. As a result, predicting the performance of sim2real transfer for a specific model is not possible. To address this limitation, we present a study where we evaluate the transferability of models entered into the NeurIPS 2020 Autonomous Driving Challenge. Through our analysis, we uncover connections between specific attributes of virtual training data and the ability to transfer learning in real-world scenarios. Although our focus is on image-based tasks, our findings offer insights that can be applied to other domains where sim2real transfer is utilized. Our work highlights the complexity of sim2real transfer and emphasizes the need for a systematic approach to evaluating the effectiveness of sim2real transfer for any model.

The sophistication of deepfakes is rising swiftly, with the breathtaking quality of the average deepfake video astounding users and convincing many of its authenticity - the majority of surveyed individuals cannot tell whether a watermarked video is authentic or not. While deepfakes pose no inherent threat to society, the proliferation of politically charged and socially significant deepfakes poses a significant risk of causing harm, spreading misinformation, and influenceling public opinion and electoral outcomes. Given the rapid advancement of deepfake technology, it is crucial to develop effective countermeasures not just to detect deepfakes, but to mitigate their spread and the resulting harm they cause. Our proposed solution centers on watermarking - a long-established technique first demonstrated in 1995 by Andrew Wappner and I. J. Good, with potential to be scaled up to tenfold with the integration of new methods, such as learning-based approaches. Our research evaluates the effectiveness of watermarking in preventing the spread of deepfakes, with particular focus on their detection and prevention in online spaces. Ultimately, we argue that the most pressing issue related to deepfakes is not their creation, but their widespread dissemination - a problem that can be tackled in large part by preventing the spread of deepfake media through the implementation of effective watermarking technologies.

The diverse range of atmospheres on exoplanets, particularly those on temperate planets with masses significantly smaller or larger than Earth, is not yet thoroughly understood. To gain insights into the differences between small and massive atmospheres on temperate planets, scientists have been using various theoretical models and analyzing how atmospheric compositions form. Throughout this study, researchers found that a key factor influencing atmospheric composition is the planet's mass, leading to distinct carbon and nitrogen gas patterns. In atmospheres surrounding less massive planets, carbon and nitrogen are absorbed into various compounds and lose their elementary form. In contrast, atmospheres surrounding more massive planets experience a different trapping mechanism for short-wave radiation, resulting in higher surface temperatures and reduced volatility of carbon and nitrogen-containing compounds. As a consequence, the atmospheres of massive planets are enriched with carbon and nitrogen, whereas those of less massive planets contain lower volumes of carbon and nitrogen, which often end up in the planet's interior. To further accurately predict atmospheric compositions, scientists must also consider other factors such as the planet's thermal inheritance and dynamic atmospheric circulation. The study provides a solid theoretical foundation for future observations aimed at validating model predictions and contributing to a deeper understanding of exoplanet atmospheres.

The McCulloch-Pitts network, an evolution of the Hopfield network, has been discovered to be capable of replicating the stable memory states of its predecessor. Interestingly, this replication capability comes with the cost of limiting the learning capacity of the McCulloch-Pitts network compared to the Hopfield network. Researchers found that the largest number of learnable patterns in the McCulloch-Pitts network is twice the number allowed in the Hopfield network. Despite its limitations, the McCulloch-Pitts network remains an essential component in advanced neural network architectures and is vital for understanding computational neuroscience. The findings presented in this study provide a quantitative explanation for the prevalence of local nonflat areas in the network's parameter space, leading to a new hypothesis initially supported by numerical data and theoretical analysis, which suggests that these areas are directly responsible for the network's stable memory states.

This paper proposes a new dataset, called Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV), consisting of a comprehensive collection of scene text images with significant errors mimicking real-world mistakes encountered in current end-to-end scene text recognition models. The OOV dataset includes two distinct error types: the replacement error, where words are replaced with irrelevant terms, and the corruption error, featuring distorted and unreadable text. Researchers have shown that leveraging datasets like OOV can enhance the robustness and effectiveness of scene text recognition models, and the dataset is available at https://github.com/SoMinShu/OOV_Dataset.

Numerical methods for analyzing parameter-dependent systems can involve multiple possible solutions, with some isolated and others connected by transition paths. By using the smoothly varying nature of these systems, previously estimated via nonlinear analysis, we propose a new, hybrid approach. This approach combines precise numerical calculations for confirmed solution branches with transitional path predictions, generated through a variant of the local perturbations method. Unlike other predictive methods, our approach validates the predicted solution branches, ensuring their accuracy before considering transition paths. This difference is significant, as it allows our algorithm to focus on finding transitional paths for systems with a large number of possible solutions, by leveraging previously computed solution branches and their validity. As a result, we are able to efficiently compute all isolated solutions for a particular system of differential equations with a high number of parameters.

This research addresses the critical issues of change point detection and failure
mode isolation by developing an innovative method with significantly reduced
computational complexity. Currently, detecting changes and identifying failure
modes within a system produces vast amounts of data that becomes difficult to
analyze, especially when equipped with limited computational resources. Two
key challenges arise: dynamically detecting anomalies and pinpointing the source
of these anomalies. Building on techniques from statistical physics and using
sparsity as a model assumption, a powerful framework is introduced to efficiently
detect changes and isolate failures even in highly complex systems. In this
research, we illustrate the effectiveness of this new method by detecting changes
and identifying failures in synthetic data, predictive models, and real-world datasets.

We have conducted a detailed analysis of the ages of star clusters within two smaller galactic building blocks attached to the Milky Way, namely the Gaia-Sausage Enceladus and Wukong/LMS-1 systems. We used this data to follow the development of star formation within these components over time and compared it to earlier studies based on different data, including star colors and motions. Our research revealed that star formation within the Gaia-Sausage Enceladus system likely lasted for at least 2 billion years, whereas it took less than 2 billion years for the system Wukong/LMS-1 to form. We also discovered that the majority of star clusters within the Gaia-Sausage Enceladus system were involved in large-scale star formation episodes about 8.9 billion years ago that also influenced the development of similar systems including Berglund 5, Segue 11, and Hyades. Conversely, the ages of star clusters within the Wukong/LMS-1 system do not indicate any significant star formation episodes in the system. Instead, Gaia-Sausage Enceladus and Berglund 5 are thought to be in the midst of transitioning from merger activity to globular cluster formation, whereas Enceladus and Berglund 5 both host younger generations of stars formed more recently.

Machine learning models need extensively labeled training data to perform accurately, but creating this data is time-consuming, leading to a limitation known as data scarcity. A technique called selective labeling aims to address this issue by allocating labeling resources to specific instances more efficiently, as it only requires labeling unlabelled data instances that are particularly difficult to classify. This study explores the effectiveness of selective labeling by adopting a Bayesian perspective, and developing methods to implement it through threshold-based policies, reinforcement learning, and deep neural network training. Experimental evaluations are conducted across various datasets and models to compare different policy approaches.

Various devices leveraging spin-orbit torques have been created with an indium arsenide interface, yet the essential properties of this interface remain poorly understood. Our study focuses on the interface between europium sulfide and indium arsenide and investigates its electronic structure through high-resolution spectroscopy and computational models. High-resolution valence band spectroscopy reveals a unique sub-band maximum near the valence band start on the europium sulfide side of the interface, which is in line with theoretical models and density functional calculations. Our analysis shows how dispersed states from the europium sulfide valence band maximum contribute to the interface's electronic structure, while the absence of dispersive states from the indium arsenide start indicates that the interface's electronic structure is primarily defined by the europium sulfide. Ultimately, our findings support the use of surface-science-based approaches to design and develop improved spin-orbit torques in microelectronics and other technologies.

We establish a specific consequence of Borel Wadge determinacy, which in turn has significant implications for second-order arithmetic. Specifically, it implies the proof of $\text{True Arithmetic}$ being the unique minimal model of arithmetic, thereby making $\text{True Arithmetic}$ computationally closed.

Recent advancements in click trainability have made it possible to achieve efficient training and deployment of Neural Network architectures, overcoming the challenges posed by the discrepancy between the computational complexity of training and inference. In order to bridge this gap, researchers use various methods such as pruning, quantization, and other techniques. Among these, pruning has gained significant attention due to its ability to substantially decrease memory and processing costs during inference. However, most current pruning techniques focus on improving the training-inference discrepancy by regulating the gradient smoothing and setosa distribution, rather than directly addressing the discrepancy itself. In this research, a novel approach is presented to directly address the training-inference discrepancy and improve the accuracy of the inference process. We developed ClickTrain, a click-based training framework based on stochastic click regularization that promotes discrete gradient distribution and reduces memorization effects. As a result, ClickTrain demonstrates significant improvement in inference performance compared to traditional pruning methods, alongside a pronounced pruning-effect relationship. We achieved top-tier results on the ImageNet dataset when comparing ClickTrain to other state-of-the-art pruning techniques.

We establish a relational semantics that is equivalent to existing semantics for substructural modal logics in its various forms. This semantics serves as a foundation for cut-elimination proofs in these logics, and its properties enable the direct application of relational semantics techniques to the study of modal logic as a whole.

The merger of gravitationalley bound objects, such as neutron stars, emits spectral patterns that vary freely responsive to the temporal occurrence and movement of the source. Observations of electromagnetic and gravitational waves simultaneously provide crucial insight into neutron star coalescence events, significantly increasing our understanding of these events compared to individual wave observations. To explore neutron star mergers detectable through both gravitational and electromagnetic radiation, we updated the Binary Pulse Model, incorporating neutron star merger data, and applied it to forecast observables during and after the merger. The updated model, informed by LIGO and Virgo's observations to date, accounts for the initial 100 seconds of the merger, and it incorporates analysis of the merger's electromagnetic spectrum, covering the initial 10 seconds. The model enables the computation of several key observables, including spectral powers, polarization properties, and gravitational wave amplitude during and after the merger. Furthermore, we outline potential research outcomes from future observations, including those possible with the next generation of gravitational wave detectors, and we highlight the significant advancements that simultaneous observation of gravitational and electromagnetic radiation provides compared to individual wave observations.

Substellar objects that form around white dwarfs offer a unique setting for analyzing planetary composition and formation. The recently discovered planet, TOI-5542b, orbiting a white dwarf in the Kepler mission, presents an intriguing opportunity for conducting detailed analysis of its composition, potentially revolutionizing our understanding of planetary evolution theory. TOI-5542b's radius and mass measurements suggest it is an unsually large, possibly hydrogen-rich sub-Neptune planet or a late-stage planetary remnant. To further understand the planet's composition, we employed two independent methods to determine its density, using the transmission photometry data from the TESS sector 6 observations and the Spitzer space telescope's data at two separate wavelengths. The resulting density estimates range from 0.26 to 0.35 gram per cubic centimeter, with the planet's composition likely involving a substantial H/He component. The subsequent modeling indicates that a massive hydrogen layer is necessary to explain the planet's observed radius, with the possible presence of a solid core. The discovered density range significantly surpasses traditional rocky planet density profiles, with high-pressure magnesium oxide ice dominating the composition of any solid core. The massive H/He component in TOI-5542b might have originated from envelope accretion or was preserved due to the late completion of accretion.

This study presents a groundbreaking sampling-based SDP algorithm that efficiently solves complex stochastic submodular optimization problems, featuring a novel operational cost function. In practical applications, this approach can be utilized to develop issue-focused operational policies by solving a multi-objective optimization problem that balances the objectives of minimizing waste and maximizing revenue. Our research showcases the effectiveness of this new algorithm, outperforming existing solutions on a range of empirical benchmarks.

We've developed a k-Nearest Neighbors classifier tailored for recognizing mathematical symbols within an informal setting. The system, inspired by the k-Nearest Neighbors classifier used by Jason Naradowski in his 2008 Ph.D. research, boasts a concise implementation that can even operate on embedded systems. We've successfully put this classifier to use in two applications: one for recognizing mathematical symbols, and another for translating handwritten digits. Our mathematical symbol recognition application demonstrates a striking 99% accuracy rate, effectively reducing the complexity of model training by eliminating the need for class balances and model updates. In contrast, the handwritten digit recognition application achieves a remarkable 95.5% accuracy rate, surpassing the performance of leading external deep learning models, yet requires only a minuscule 5 MB of memory.

Understanding and measuring network complexity has become a crucial aspect in predicting and managing epidemic spreading. We have developed a ground-breaking method to quantify network complexity through the calculation of entropy based on the topology of connections between nodes. By applying the concept of relative entropy, we compare the probability distribution of node infections to an uniform distribution, thereby creating a set of observable values called 'bridgeness' that measures the likelihood of epidemic spreading. Our study of bridgeness in two typical complex networks - a scale-free network and a small-world network - demonstrates that entropy is highly responsive to the network's characteristics, particularly its mean degree and clustering coefficient. Furthermore, our results show that extreme values of bridgeness are found in networks with central characteristics, thereby identifying 'bottlenecks' that may impede or accelerate the spread of epidemics.

In reinforcement learning, safety rules can prevent crashes but sometimes
predicting all possible hazards is impractical. Currently used methods, such as
additive-safety or robustness-certification approaches, either restrict large
steps or guarantee minimal compliance, often limiting progress. In contrast,
this research introduces an alternative, which seeks to learn both safe and
efficient paths by incorporating uncertainty from constraint conditions into the action choice process. By certifying the safety of each action before taking it, this method reduces the likelihood of violations and surpasses previous performance in similar tests.

We develop a concept, twin identity, to identify twin primes by considering the relationship between their underlying geometric objects, called elliptic curves, for which we provide analytical proof and establish a fundamental theorem. Additionally, we introduce $k$-twin identities covering sets of multiple primes collectively known as $k$-twin primes and provide a generalization of the fundamental theorem for $k$-twin identities through the application of the Chebotarev density theorem.

This research paper introduces a pioneering layered control system that integrates
machine learning with control theory to empower mobile platforms with advanced
navigation capabilities, specifically in scenarios involving sonar sensors for mapping
purposes. Our key innovation is a multi-agent control structure, with a high-level
module guiding data flow and interaction, and two core modules leveraging ML models
and control systems, respectively, to inform each other and facilitate self-awareness.
Through this synergy, the system achieves a dynamic balance between exploration and
mapping, resulting in efficient robot operation. Our approach demonstrates its bold
ideas through simulations, demonstrating the system's ability to adapt to shifting
sensor configurations and outperform traditional benchmark methods.

We've obtained a unique photometric measurement of Nereid, a small icy object on the edge of the solar system that only appears bright enough to be detected every 60 years. This rare observation was captured on January 30, 2021. Combining our data with previously obtained infrared images from Spitzer and Hubble, we obtained a comprehensive spectral dataset spanning the range from 0.2 to 4.5 micrometers. This analysis reveals that Nereid's surface is characterized by two distinct spectral slopes, similar to other icy objects in the solar system's outer regions, such as Triton and Arrokoth. This suggests that Nereid's surface is composed of water ice, probably mixed with a layer of methane and tholins, a type of organic material. Our findings present the most detailed insight into Triton's tiny companion since Nereid's close-up images taken by Voyager 2 in 1989.

We establish a connection between the projective plane's geometric properties and certain algebraic characteristics of its underlying ring, drawing on the relationship between affine planes and projective planes constructed from the projective line over a ring. Furthermore, we define a category structure among these planes based on ring homomorphisms that preserve the *-involution, and demonstrate that the projective plane over a ring is indeed a well-defined projective plane.

This note outlines a technique developed by D. Mejía, M. Tomás, and M. Tomás's students, for demonstrating the proof of certain implications between different cardinal characteristics in set theory within a specific order framework. The Tukey-order was initially introduced as a method for comparing uniform spaces through Tukey reductions, later generalized to other categories of mathematical structures. Although the concept was primarily discussed using models of specific axioms, its applications extend to various sets of sentences. The method has proven particularly effective for certain cardinal characteristics in set theory, providing straightforward proofs of certain implications and limiting others. Notably, the method has helped resolve long-standing open problems in the field.

Integrating the pessimism principle into Thompson sampling yields a more robust method for optimizing dynamic treatment policies, even in complex situations where the utility function and treatment effects are uncertain and potentially incorrect. We have developed an interquartile range (IQR) credible interval, a type of predictive interval, to address this concern. Drawing on the pessimism principle, this IQR interval ensures that the estimated treatment effect is likely to be magnified rather than diminished, thereby providing a more conservative estimate. The pessimism principle, integrated with Thompson sampling, maintains exploratory efficiency while offering heightened defensive value against adverse conditions. The combination of pessimism and empirical Bayesian methods results in a more reliable IQR interval, even in the presence of skewed data. Notably, the pessimism principle's impact on the IQR interval is most pronounced for treatment effects with wider confidence intervals - exactly the scenarios where uncertainty is most acute. The pessimism principle's benefits extend to standard Thompson sampling as well as more sophisticated models, like random forests and neural networks.

We determine the asymptotic scale at which invariance of K-groups beyond K0 is maintained for an algebra or a Z-graded algebra, given a subcategory of modules with finite generation. Furthermore, a subcategory's invariance in K-groups is not dependent on the algebra's extending property when the subcategory consists of modules of a certain degree. This has a significant implication in the invariance of K-groups for certain types of group algebras and C* algebras. Additionally, a subcategory's invariance in K-groups can be applied to calculate the groups for certain partially ordered sets and band C* algebras. Finally, we provide invariance results for K-groups for Hermitian modules of a specific degree and rank.

We introduce a generalized framework for classifying quantum states based on multiple arrays of probabilistic predictions that remain consistent with quantum mechanics. Our method allows for the identification of connections between distinct arrangements of quantum states, which can be linked through a series of intermediate steps. We demonstrate that arrays of probabilistic predictions can serve as a comprehensive representation of quantum states, and we establish a formal relationship between the concept of nonlocality in Bell scenarios and contextuality in matrix modules. Our framework facilitates the identification of relationships between distinct arrangements of quantum states, which can be linked through a series of intermediate steps. We illustrate the effectiveness of our approach by examining arrays of probabilistic predictions associated with qubit states, as well as with higher-dimensional states known as SIC (Stimson's Incredible Dimensional) states.

Researchers examine the pairing in a multiband Hubbard model with an
exact eta-pairing ground state across various bandwidths and fillings.
Unlike single-band models, the strength of pairing in the multiband model
peaks beyond half-filling, occurring at filling parameters $n=2+(1/\eta)$,
where $\eta$ represents the anomaly parameter within the ground state's phase
transition. At this filling, odd-band electrons form a degenerate set of
single-band spectra, allowing for a smooth transition to a strong pairing
state. We discover that within a certain range of bandwidths, the ground
state exhibits both $d_{x^2-y^2}$ and $d_{xz}$ pairing correlations,
originating from distinct correlation components, whereas outside a critical
point, the dominant pairing correlation shifts to $d_{x^2-y^2}$.

We address the $p$-adic analog of the generalized Polya theorem. Specifically, we solve a key functional equation using the properties of functions on $\beta$-adics, where the domain is a $p$-adic solenoid. Our method relies on the continuous $p$-adic analysis framework. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any given $p$-adic continuous function, defined on a certain type of $p$-adic group, can be decomposed into a finite sum of $p$-adic automorphic functions.

Unsupervised classification methods for species presence-absence data often struggle with overlapping clusters and sub-clustering. New approaches aim to address these challenges, but a comprehensive evaluation of different solutions is still needed. In this research, we assessed the performance of seven novel techniques alongside established methods to determine which ones successfully recover simulated clusters of varying complexity. These techniques include non-parametric clustering with Bayesian binary regression, Bayesian binary autoencoders, hierarchical clustering of similarities, shared nearest neighbors, Gaussian mixture models, Dirichlet process mixtures, and hierarchical Gaussian mixture models. We investigated the influence of cluster density, number of clusters, and data dimensionality on clustering outcomes and examined the correlation between predicted probabilities and cluster assignments. Our results indicate that Bayesian binary regression, shared nearest neighbors, and Gaussian mixture models consistently perform well across different cluster configurations, while other methods face limitations, particularly in identifying and recovering sparse clusters. We also observed that predicted probabilities and cluster assignments are increasingly correlated as cluster densities rise. This research provides a thorough understanding of the capabilities and shortcomings of various clustering methods, offering practitioners a solid foundation for selecting the most suitable methods for their specific data analysis needs.

RGB-RGBD unified salient object detection aims to handle various color and depth image modalities effectively, although existing approaches often neglect dimensionality reduction's efficiency and learnable feature sharing. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a unified deep feature fusion framework, featuring learnable feature transformation and a dual-layer fusion mechanism. By integrating image modality embedding and activating, our method enhances representation efficiency and produces more precise salient maps. Given its versatility, our approach outperforms other state-of-the-art methods in multiple segmentation benchmarks, even when dealing with real-world RGB-D datasets. The code can be found at https://github.com/SMU-LucyTeam/Unified_RGB-RGBD_Salient_Object_Detection.

We've participated in the SemEval 2019 Task 6 Data Subtask A competition, where the goal was to identify abusive tweets with high accuracy and ignore neutral content. Our approach to the challenge involved creating a dataset from scratch to tap into the implicit knowledge present in the data. Our training technique leveraged deep learning and included data augmentation, while our inference process utilized a memory-augmented neural network architecture. With a macro F1 score of 0.774, we successfully outranked several other competing teams and secured the top ranking in the competition.

Eugenio González and Ignacio Montón developed a proof that the set of integers that cannot be represented using a given base and a fixed number of digits has a positive density. They also established that this property holds for an infinite number of representations. A similar result was found for palindromic numbers, meaning numbers that remain the same when their digits are reversed, in a specific base. Nonetheless, there exists a non-palindromic number for every base greater than 2. The significance of these results lies in their applicability not just to representations involving a single base but also to combinations of multiple bases. The found representations are often shorter than those previously known to exist. The proof follows Carmichael's original argument but requires additional reasoning for numbers with a mixed representation. The found representations are often shorter than those previously known to exist. The paper concludes by addressing a question about the existence of a non-palindromic number for every base greater than 2, which has been answered in the affirmative.

To overcome the limitations of conventional methods in dealing with mixed noise during CT imaging, we introduce a novel deep learning framework. Utilizing a hybrid noise model, the proposed network is able of accurately estimating both quantum noise and systematic error in its input, followed by a training process using the limited angle Shepp-Logan phantom. The model is then assessed using the numerical limited angle Hartmann-Steppes transform and simulated CT scans, where its performance is compared to the industry-standard TV-regularized expectation-maximization algorithm. Our results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed model over TV-regularized expectation-maximization algorithm, notably in its ability to handle various noise levels without being retrained.

Bayesian Program Learning represents programs as distributions of executable code, simplifying the search process for program variants. We apply this concept to the generation of handwritten images and demonstrate that BL can produce natural-looking output samples with just one training example, drawing inspiration from the effective use of prior knowledge and regularization in traditional machine learning. Unlike existing generative models, BL bypasses the complexity of learning intricate models and instead employs a prior distribution to guide the search within the program's search space. Additionally, BL's program variants are unique, providing control over the generated output through arbitrary inputs. In our experiments, we used a 1-layer CNN-based generator module based on a discrete image representation, combined with a residual frame generation method to produce continuous images, and applied a normalizing flow to transform the program distribution into a more manageable form. The implementation is available on our GitHub page.

A newly devised storage technique substantially reduces memory usage when creating three-nucleon interaction matrix elements, effectively lowering the memory burden from cubic to quadratic scale. This advancement enables the exhaustive generation of all possible three-nucleon interaction matrix elements within a predetermined basis, without relying on pre-computed data or spatial symmetries. The novel storage method also accelerates the process by shifting the bottleneck from memory access to arithmetic operations on the central processor unit.

In the past year, our group has made significant breakthroughs in the application of quantum electronics. Two key techniques, the correlator method and the von-Neumann density-matrix method, have been used to compute advanced full-counting events and study quantum-coherence phenomena. These methods have enabled us to analyze semi-conductor quantum pumps, Josephson junctions, and topological islands with an unprecedented level of detail. Furthermore, we have extended the principles of entanglement, originally applied to quantum optics and Jordan-algebra theory, to the domain of quantum electronics, while drawing interesting connections between the two areas. These findings have been published in prominent scientific journals, and we present them in the form of a single, unified narrative, with the aim of illuminating the role of entanglement in the context of quantum electronics.

This study investigates non-isomorphic bounded convex domains in C^n that are analytic transformations of each other, focusing on how the properties of composition operators change between these domains when the mapping is not straightforward.  It turns out that the presence of non-trivial analytic discs in the domain's boundary affects the injectivity and boundedness of the composition operator when the disc's 1 or 2-dimensional projection is involved, while real analytic discs within a specific context influence compactness as well as surjectivity and its absence.

In string theory, a specific kernel related to four-twist operators is crucial in determining the structure of a particular operator, known as the "penalty operator," which appears in the string spectrum. We've analyzed the two-loop corrections to the penalty operator's anomalous dimensions and found that they are subject to a specific scaling equation, one that can be solved to yield an exact value for the operator's structure, a result that can then be used to solve the penalty operator's scaling equation exactly. We also determined the loop-corrected penalty operator and found that it converges to a specific, exact value at three loops. We compared our results to the loop-corrected penalty operator calculated using gauge/gravity correspondence and found that the two methods yield similar results for the penalty operator's structure, a result that can be used to make precise predictions about the penalty operator's behavior at high values of a special variable "s."

Most deep learning frameworks allocate memory independently for computation and activation buffers on the GPU, but this can lead to excessive memory waste and slow reallocation. Our new framework, DynaSOAr, addresses these issues by using a single, unified array to cache all memory pools, streamlining the allocation process and improving both memory efficiency and runtime performance. In addition to optimizing memory allocation, DynaSOAr also includes a second layer of optimization that automatically detects and exploits overlapping patterns in computation and activation buffers, further reducing memory requirements. By combining efficient memory management with intelligent buffer management, DynaSOAr demonstrates significant improvements over traditional allocators, reducing memory allocation time and decreasing memory usage by as much as 2x and 1.5x respectively, without sacrificing accuracy.

We investigate the possibility of isospin violation in dark matter detection, focusing on the $b \rightarrow s$ process, to resolve the tension between direct detection experiments and the Standard Model prediction for the dark matter nucleus cross section. To achieve isospin violation, we introduce a mediating vector boson, $X$, with a non-unity coupling to the $b-X$ vertex, along with an isolation mediator scenario where $X$ does not couple to other quarks. This development incorporates a light $X$ with mass less than 30 GeV, characterized by a narrow decay width, and leads to the generation of isospin violation through differing form factors of the $d$ and $s$ quarks. Furthermore, we determine the allowed parameter space of $X$, a scalar or vector boson, by considering the constraints from $b \rightarrow s$ transition, LHC data, and dark matter direct detection, including the recently released XENON1T data for single-hit events. We observe that while the model is capable of addressing the $b \rightarrow s$ process and LHC data constraints, it remains subject to a significant gap between theoretical and experimental cross sections for dark matter nucleus interactions. This gap is bridged by data from p+p bar collisions at low-energy scales, as well as by data from beam dump experiments. Additionally, we have found that the model is compatible with neutrino mass generation at a few GeV and leaves room for a viable

Straw tube detectors utilized in particle physics research are subjected to vacuum conditions that cause a straw wall to contract, creating tension within the material. The minimum pre-tension required to sustain this contraction depends on straw tube parameters such as wall material, diameter, length, and thickness. In this study, an analytical model is developed to calculate this minimum pre-tension as a function of these physical properties under a uniform internal pressure. Additionally, the simulation results from finite element method tools are compared with analytical model predictions to validate their accuracy and applicability.

We suggest a way to measure the reliability of a regression model's choices
in situations where the dependent variable's distribution is uncertain.
Our method involves calculating a maximum possible loss resulting from
predicting decisions according to the model's parameters when the true parameters
differ from those used in training.
We then developed an approximation of this quantity using the training data and
proposed an algorithm for estimating its value through convex programming.
In addition, we provided an example that demonstrates the reliability of the
estimated robustness model as well as its advantage over other methods, like those
that rely on the difference between training and testing data sets.
Finally, we presented some experiments using the robustness estimate, which
show it to be more resilient to changes in data than other reliability metrics.

The oscillatory movement of an impurity within a supersolid is studied under the influence of strong interactions with surrounding quasiparticles, and its impact on phonon mode behavior is examined using Green's function approach. As the impurity's movement becomes more frequent, compared to a stationary impurity, the roton minimum's frequency decreases and the damping rate increases, and these changes persist even at lower temperatures where the impurity's movement becomes thermally activated. Furthermore, the impurity's oscillatory movement enhances the supersolid's phonon anomaly compared to the effect of static impurities, and the associated damping rate is proportional to the frequency of the anomalous phonons.

A comprehensive classification system for neighbour-transitive codes in quadrangles and dual quadrangles has been developed, providing an extensive framework that encompasses and extends previous work on classification efforts for sotag-transitive codes in quadrangles and dual quadrangles by various researchers. The contribution extends beyond quadrangles to include Weyl duals, which are dual quadrangles, and it also generalises to polar duals of quadrangles and dual quadrangles. The classification system defines neighbour-transitive codes through their behaviour under neighbourhood operations and by transitivity properties, then expresses these classifications using stabiliser graphs, which are derived based on point and line stabilisers in the quadrangles and their duals. The study of neighbour-transitive codes in quadrangles and their duals has been completed, and it has been shown that there are no neighbour-transitive codes of rank 2 in quadrangles and their duals beyond the known examples of [8,4,3] codes. In contrast, it has been found that there are numerous neighbour-transitive codes of various ranks in the Weyl duals of quadrangles and their duals.

We performed a comprehensive investigation of the density pattern within a specific area of our Galaxy's central region, using extensive molecular gas data from various sources, encompassing all available observations up to 2011. By integrating the observed data at different density levels and applying a sophisticated density estimation method, we generated a comprehensive density map of the study area on multiple scales. Our findings indicate that as the scale decreases, the anisotropy in the density structure's overall pattern increases, contradicting earlier expectations. A rigorous analysis revealed that the primary source driving this outcome is the presence of a dense molecular cloud, specifically Complex C, which strongly influences the 2D density pattern and causes it to deviate from the area's overall radial velocity pattern. Furthermore, our research shows that the area's density and velocity patterns exhibit distinct discontinuities at scales below 100 pc, suggesting that the patterns are decentralized and instead follow the path of the area's velocity gradient. We hypothesize that the cloud's impact is a critical factor in explaining the area's density and velocity behavior and the cloud's effect on the area's disk-like pattern.

We conducted an experimental study on the non-linear absorption properties of metallic nickel at a 800 nm wavelength, utilizing a high-repetition-rate femtosecond laser with variable pulse energies and a range of fluences going up from hundreds of millijoules per square centimeter. To compare theory with experiment, the results were normalized by accounting for electron redistribution and considering both inter-band and intra-band electron transitions as described by the Drude model and semi-classical Taylor expansion methods, across a range of metal densities. It was observed in the experiments that nickel exhibits a significant change from linear to non-linear absorption behavior at around 10 Jouares per square centimeter fluence, and this shift is caused by a rapid increase in the non-linear third-order absorption coefficient as fluence increases. This increase in absorption is attributed to electron redistribution and changes in the Drude dielectric function at high fluences, leading to a rapid rise in the non-linear component when the dielectric function starts to deviate significantly from its initial state. This phenomenon results in a significant change from linear to non-linear absorption behavior at high fluences and may provide a mechanism for self-modulation of laser-matter interactions in nickel and other metals with similar properties.

A tiny camera sensor with the ability to measure temperature has around 1000 pixels, and it can determine temperature differences between objects with accuracy better than typical sensor specifications, by analyzing shadows in thermal images. To improve its performance, this sensor uses machine learning to analyze these images and account for variations in lighting and the movement of objects, all without the need for additional equipment or processing power. Testing has shown that this sensor can successfully measure the temperature differences between objects in scenarios both with and without the presence of the sun, and even when objects are partially obscured.

A combination of single-photon techniques, including quantum scissors and
single-photon interferometry, enables the creation of complex entangled states
among multiple polarized photons. By utilizing the quantum scissors technique to
generate a Bell state from a single-photon interferometer, and then interacting
the Bell state with additional photons within a micro-wave cavity, researchers
have successfully produced two-photon entangled states. This approach has the
advantage of producing fewer errors compared to traditional methods, while also
producing a wider variety of complex entangled states.

The basic model for distributing shortest paths in graph spanner construction involves a network of nodes where distance between any two points is exact in the optimal Steiner tree, or a closer approximation called a delta, within a fixed multiple of the optimal distance. In the online version of this problem, the algorithm creates the spanner one edge at a time without knowing future additions to the network, and the optimal Steiner tree at any point in time. It's been shown that a competitive ratio of O(log^2 n) is achievable and indeed optimal in the planar graph scenario. Furthermore, for graphs of any n nodes with edge weight mean degree d, a ratio of O(log^2 n / log d) is achievable and optimal when delta equals the optimal distance, and optimal distance multiplied by a constant for a given subset of the network. In the general case with edge weights uniformly distributed between one and n, a competitive ratio of O(log^2 n) is achievable and optimal in the online version where the Steiner point cost is linear, and a ratio of O(log^2 n / log m) is achievable and optimal when the cost for a given subset of the network is proportional to the number of points included. In dimensions higher than three, a ratio of O(log^2 n) is achievable and optimal when the cost for a given subset of the network is linear, and a ratio of O(log^2 n) is achievable and optimal when the cost for a given subset of the

This research explores the possibility of misclassifying IoT devices by taking into account their classification as secure or malicious with a cost in mind. Initially, we outline various cost models that could lead to device misclassification and identify situations in which this becomes feasible. We then propose a decision-making strategy, based on Bayesian analysis, that can purposefully misclassify devices at the expense of increased overall classification cost. This approach can be optimized for either individual or group gains. We further investigate the potential for a system of devices to collectively misclassify themselves in a game theoretical context, with a focus on the most effective strategies for both the system and an external classifier. Finally, we introduce the concept of 'leverage', a measure of the potential for a group of devices to intentionally misclassify themselves, and we establish a corresponding upper limit through comprehensive analysis of various cost models.

This study provides a comprehensive description of finite G\"odel algebras in relation to their duals, analogous to the finite forest's structure, and as a result, establishes an isomorphism between the structure of finite G\"odel algebras and the structure of finite forests under the filtration method. To achieve this, we introduce an iterative compression method to derive an explicit representation of finite G\"odel algebras in terms of cardinalities of specific free G\"odel algebras, and through an inductive reasoning based on cardinality, we achieve the desired result.

We develop a parametric aligner, Aligner, capable of being trained on multiple
corpora and adapted to various tasks such as morphological alignment, word
alignment, and translation alignment. By formulating these tasks as a specific
alignment type, Aligner can tackle them without requiring task-specific
algorithms. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Aligner by training it on a
smaller corpus and achieving similar results to established aligners like GIZA++.
Moreover, Aligner exhibits better performance in translation alignment compared to
GIZA++, particularly in a low-data scenario. The source code is freely accessible
on GitHub at https://github.com/guntherpx/Aligner.

This paper presents a asynchronous block-iterative decomposition algorithm. By combining the Krasnoselskii-Mann iteration method and the extrapolation technique, the proposed method draws on fixed point theory. An equivalent formulation of the algorithm involves finding a common fixed point of a collection of operators, which facilitates the application of Banach fixed point theorem. We investigate the convergence of the algorithm and provide conditions for its effective operation in the context of nonexpansive maps. Furthermore, the method's efficiency is demonstrated through its application to a telecommunication network problem.

Our research involves simulating microlensing events caused by primordial black holes (PBH) that occur when a PBH passes in front of a variable star at a specific distance.
